data.title: Middle East Eye: UK awards deals worth millions to firms linked to illegal Israeli settlements
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
UK awards deals worth millions to firms linked to illegal Israeli settlements
The British government has awarded £10.7m ($14.4m) in public contracts to firms linked to illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, it has emerged.
The contracts were published after Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced comprehensive sanctions on the settlements on 8 September in parliament, according to an Al Jazeera investigation.
"To those who finance or facilitate illegal settlements, let me say this: you will face the full force of UK sanctions," Miliband said. "Settlements are illegal."
But the sanctions have not yet come into force and implementing them could take up to nine months, according to government sources.
In the meantime, the government has awarded two contracts worth about £87,900 ($118,000) to Motorola Solutions and its subsidiaries to provide communications for the police, Al Jazeera reported.

data.title: Middle East Eye: ‘We woke up soaking wet’: Gaza’s displaced face another winter of floods and collapsed shelters
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
‘We woke up soaking wet’: Gaza’s displaced face another winter of floods and collapsed shelters
For the past four days, Nahla al-Majdoub, 48, and her family of eight have been staying with neighbours in the west of Gaza City after their tent was destroyed by the latest heavy rainfall.
Majdoub and her family had been sheltering in a makeshift tent at the port of Gaza for nearly two years after their home in the northern Gaza Strip was destroyed during Israel’s ground invasion.
But when heavy rain and strong winds swept across the besieged enclave last week, their fragile shelter could no longer protect them.
They were asleep when the storm began. They woke to the sound of thunder and rainwater pouring into their shelter, seeping through the roof and flooding the ground beneath their tent.
“I woke up soaking wet. I looked at my children, who were also wet and surrounded by water. We cried helplessly, not knowing what to do or how to protect them,” Majdoub said.

data.author: Rikki Sprinzak
data.summary:
The changing face of Israel’s ultra-Orthodox politics
Submitted by
Rikki Sprinzak
on
Tue, 11/10/2026 - 10:35
Election results expose growing divisions within Haredi society and raise questions about the future of its longstanding alliance with Netanyahu
One of the most significant developments in the aftermath of the Israeli elections was the decision by United Torah Judaism (UTJ), the main ultra-Orthodox Jewish party, not to recommend Benjamin Netanyahu to form the next government.
This marks a departure from years of close alliance between Netanyahu and the ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, parties, long considered a pillar of Israeli politics.
Even if the move was tactical, intended to strengthen the Haredi parties’ bargaining position, it sends an important signal, as last month’s vote exposed several significant shifts within Haredi society.
They include the declining standing of veteran political leaders, a struggle over the future of Haredi leadership, the emergence of a new political force challenging established conventions from within, and a deepening crisis surrounding the model of the “society of learners”.
This social model developed in Israel, where Torah study in yeshivas and kollelim has become a central way of life and even a social ideal for Haredi men. Many devote years to religious study instead of entering the labour market or undertaking military service.
The model rests on the belief that Torah study is a supreme value and a communal obligation, supported financially by families, the community, the state and religious support networks.
For decades, the Haredi parties were among the most stable and predictable blocs in Israeli politics. They relied on communal loyalty, rabbinical authority, and the largely automatic voting patterns of a constituency that sought to preserve its political influence through unified Haredi representation.

The assault destroys machinery worth more than $1m and threatens the livelihoods of hundreds of Palestinian workers and their families
Settlers torched excavators, vehicles and pieces of equipment belonging to local stone-cutting workshops in Beita, near Nablus, in the occupied West Bank, 10 November 2026 (Muhammad Ateeq/MEE)

Israeli settlers attacked an industrial zone in the Palestinian town of Beita, south of Nablus in the occupied West Bank, on Monday, setting fire to heavy machinery, vehicles and equipment and causing extensive damage.
Dozens of settlers stormed the industrial zone and torched three excavators, along with several other vehicles and pieces of equipment belonging to local stone-cutting workshops.
Ashraf Ghazaly, the owner of the heavy machinery, said more than 150 settlers took part in the attack. They threw stones at Palestinian workers before storming one of the workshops and setting fire to machinery, vehicles and equipment.
Ghazaly estimated the losses at more than 3.3 million shekels (approximately $1m). One excavator had been purchased just four days earlier.
"They assaulted my brother and other workers; no one was able to stand up to them or stop them," Ghazaly told Middle East Eye.
The settlers came from the "Navitar" settlement, established on land belonging to Beita.
This latest attack is part of a series of repeated settler assaults on Beita’s industrial zone, which houses stone-cutting workshops, other businesses and heavy machinery that provide a vital source of income for dozens of families and workers in the town.
According to Ghazaly, two previous attacks in recent months involved settlers smashing the windows of bulldozers, excavators and offices.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Rubio claims Strait of Hormuz oil flows near pre-war levels on some nights
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
Rubio claims Strait of Hormuz oil flows near pre-war levels on some nights
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio says oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have recovered to more than four-fifths of their pre-war volume on some nights. He attributed the remaining shortfall to Iranian exports.
“Oil is getting out – on some nights it’s 80-85 percent of what was getting out pre-conflict.
“The only reason why it isn’t 100 percent is because Iranian oil isn’t getting out.
“The only oil that isn’t getting out consistently through the strait of Hormuz is the Iranian oil,” he told reporters at a G7 foreign ministers’ meeting in Paris.
Rubio said Washington would step up economic pressure on Tehran. “I have been told the economic campaign [against Iran] is working so well there’s no need for major combat operations,” he said.
“The economic pressure on Iran is going to get even worse,” he added.
Rubio said Washington was “open to diplomacy” to end the war, but told reporters that “the Iranian demands are totally unrealistic. We expect that could change – and if it does, we’re prepared for diplomacy.”
He said Washington could forgo further strikes “if we’re achieving the same objectives through economic means”.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israel's parliament sworn in as Eisenkot tries to forge a government
data.author: Bilge Kotan
data.summary:
Israel's parliament sworn in as Eisenkot tries to forge a government
Israel's parliament was sworn in on Tuesday without a new government, after a deadlocked general election stripped Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of his parliamentary majority but left his main rivals with no clear path to power.
Lawmakers elected in the 27 October vote took their oaths of office as Gadi Eisenkot, a former general, sought to forge a coalition after Israel's president tasked him on Sunday with forming a government.
Eisenkot and his allies also lack a majority and he has yet to strike deals with parties that could bring him to power. If both Eisenkot and Netanyahu fail to form coalitions, another election could follow.
Presiding over the swearing-in ceremony, President Isaac Herzog told lawmakers: "You must do everything to avoid a repeat election."
"Reach out a hand for compromise, even between rivals... Look upon one another with generosity. There is much work to be done here, and it requires the ability and experience found in every part of this House."

G7 foreign ministers agreed on "the need to avoid a security void" in Lebanon after UN peacekeepers pull out, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Tuesday after a meeting of the group in Paris.
They also backed "the need to move quickly toward a new security architecture" after the mandate of United Nations peacekeeping forces expires at the end of the year, he said.
But Barrot acknowledged there had been no breakthrough on what should replace the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, which has been in place since 1978 and now counts some 7,500 personnel from nearly 50 countries.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Burnham's plan to 'end neoliberalism' includes hiring US firm linked to Gaza aid site massacres
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
Burnham's plan to 'end neoliberalism' includes hiring US firm linked to Gaza aid site massacres
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has turned to an American consulting group that worked with the US and Israeli-backed Gaza Humanitarian Foundation to help draft a plan that was supposed to “end neoliberalism” in the UK.
Boston Consulting Group (BCG), whose former employees include Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Burnham’s chief of staff, James Purnell, has been hired to help shape the prime minister’s 10-year plan.
One of the “big three” management consultancy firms, BCG has been accused of aiding Israeli starvation tactics that amount to war crimes and genocide, and of being implicated in the killing of thousands of Palestinians.
The Boston-based consultancy helped establish the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF) and supported a related security company before distancing itself from the project.
The aid distribution organisation caused the death of over 2,600 Palestinians in Gaza and the injury of many thousands more. GHF ran four aid distribution sites in Gaza where Palestinians seeking aid were deliberately shot by Israeli soldiers or US security contractors hired by the organisation.

data.title: Middle East Eye: GCC to establish joint forward-command centre in Kuwait
data.author: Sean Mathews
data.summary:
GCC to establish joint forward-command centre in Kuwait
Submitted by
Sean Mathews
on
Tue, 11/10/2026 - 16:47
Given the intense attacks Kuwait has faced from Iran and its allies in Iraq, questions remain about how the new centre could be defended
Gulf Cooperation Council secretary general Jasem Mohamed al-Budaiwi gives a press conference with Russia's foreign minister and Bahrain's foreign minister after the 9th joint ministerial meeting of the strategic dialogue between the GCC and the Russian Federation in Manama, on 18 October 2026 (Fadhel Madan/AFP)
Off
The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) has approved a new joint forward-command centre to deepen military integration among members, as doubts rise about the US’s commitment to regional security amid the war on Iran.
The command centre will be built in Kuwait, a Gulf state that endured thousands of missile and drone strikes from Iran and Iraqi militias aligned with Tehran.
GCC secretary general Jasem al-Budaiwi said in a statement on Tuesday that the deployment of "appropriate" forces to the centre would take place, but did not provide additional details.
The GCC body representing six Gulf states established a joint defence agreement in 2000, stating that an attack on one member is an attack on all.
The GCC’s commitment to self-defence, however, is not as ironclad as that of the Nato military alliance.
The move could be seen as an effort to address the GCC's lack of a joint military command structure. The organisation has failed to respond to attacks on members from several fronts.
The GCC did not respond when Israel attacked Hamas negotiators in Doha, Qatar, in September 2025. The organisation has also failed to respond to devastating Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia.
The decision to base the command centre in Kuwait may also raise questions about its practical viability.

F1 star Lewis Hamilton visits Gaza border
Formula One star Lewis Hamilton visited Egypt's Rafah border crossing on Tuesday and met aid workers delivering assistance to the war-battered Gaza Strip, according to an Egyptian government statement.
North Sinai governor "Khaled Megawer took Lewis Hamilton on a visit to the Rafah land crossing to learn about the Egyptian efforts to support the Palestinian brothers in the Gaza Strip", the statement read.
Video shared by Megawer's office showed the seven-time world champion greeting aid workers and learning about their efforts to get supplies into Gaza, where this week heavy rains swept away tens of thousands of tents.
According to a truce struck by Israel and Hamas last year, at least 600 trucks of aid per day should enter Gaza, where more than two million people are facing a severe humanitarian crisis.
Aid workers say only a fraction of that amount is being allowed through by Israeli authorities, who control all entry into the territory.
Ferrari's Formula One world champion Lewis Hamilton speaks with North Sinai Governor Khaled Megawer during his visit to the Rafah border crossing between Egypt and the Gaza Strip to see firsthand efforts to receive humanitarian and relief aid bound for the Gaza Strip, in Rafah, Egypt, 10 November 2026 (Reuters)

data.title: Middle East Eye: Michigan election: How Abdul El-Sayed's critics smeared his defence of Palestinians as 'hate'
data.author: Murad Idris

Michigan election: How Abdul El-Sayed's critics smeared his defence of Palestinians as 'hate'
Submitted by
Murad Idris
on
Fri, 11/06/2026 - 20:51
By attacking his motives, the senator-elect's opponents turned a debate over US funding for Israel's genocide in Gaza into a trial of his character
Abdul El-Sayed (left) won Michigan’s US Senate seat on 3 November, two days after Haley Stevens (centre), the Democrat he beat in the primary, endorsed his Republican opponent Mike Rogers (right) (Jeff Kowalsky, Jim Watson and Blake Fagan/AFP)
Off
In his victory speech last week, Abdulrahman El-Sayed, the first Muslim American elected to the US Senate, said "hate" or "hateful" five times, and each time the word did something different.
He recalled supporters asking why he never called his opponents hateful. Those opponents, he said, "hate the idea" of an America big enough for people who pray differently.
He told Mike Rogers, the Republican he had just beaten, "You chose hate, and Michigan chose hope." Then he turned to those who call people hateful for believing that Palestinian children should not be killed with American tax dollars: "That's not hate. It's love."
In one speech, Sayed declined the word "hate", turned it around, used it as a weapon and refused it as a name. The rhetoric of hate is the currency of American politics. It gets minted, exchanged and spent, and it buys moral standing, which converts into votes and endorsements .
Everyone trades in it, including the man it was aimed at, but its real value is sorting groups into those accused of hate and those who make the accusation.
Follow its circulation through Michigan. "Hate" hounded Sayed throughout his campaign. Rogers regularly denounced his "hateful ideology". One Democrat told CNN he could not vote for Sayed "because I'm against hate".
